If you become proficient in IDE use, you’ll write a lot of code in a very little time, with very little effort! The Rider IDE catches twice as many errors as VS and has additional great features among which is advice to learners. Reading good books will enable you to know which choice to use and learn even more: Did you say syntax? Syntax-wise, although it’s similar to Java, C and C++, it has additional things that those languages lack. Those additional things make coding in C# more pleasant. And more powerful. Even so, it’s still pretty readable for an industrial-grade language. It’s even easier to learn than Python because it’s consistent, and saves you much time and headache later! Because MI leads to a lot of bugs and headache. Let’s go through a super-fast primer before seeing how C# does it better. Composition over inheritance 101 Inheritance was invented for code reuse, as the child class can use the methods and fields of the parent class. Analogically speaking, inheritance represents an “is-a” relationship. For example, a Dog is a Mammal. The class being inherited from is called the parent or superclass, and the inherited class goes by the appellation: child/subclass. Composition, on the other hand, is a design principle that deals with object relationships; it uses a “has-a” relationship. For instance, a Car has an Engine., With composition we can build complex functionalities by composing objects. It’s often a good choice when one object should own another object. Inheritance is tightly coupled, whereas composition is loosely coupled: that is, changes in the parent class in inheritance affect child classes, but changes in one class in composition don’t affect the composed classes. So C# uses composition to achieve the same. C# uses interfaces as a sort of ‘contract’ stipulating what a class can do. Let’s create an interface called ISell: Interfaces can’t implement methods (the code of what happens when you run a method). They only tell you that the ‘ISell’ interface has a .Sell() method, takes a number (integer or int) as its argument (which are how many cups are sold). Now you can guess what the IDeliver interface does: Now, we create a class. Classes represent grouped data and behavior as needed by our problem space. In the context of selling lemonade, I want to have a stand called Stand1: As you can see, on line 1, the class signs a contract with the interfaces ISell and IDeliver, promising to have the methods that those interfaces offer. Note, though, that the class Stand1 is free to decide how each interface-given method name is implemented. For instance, price is fixed (3) and delivery is within the neighborhood (15). The second stand also relies on our interfaces, but with some differences. When we sell more, price will rise. And we deliver nation-wide: Now things get interesting. The above two stands, Stand1 and Stand2 are ‘prototype’ stands, not an actual stand. They represent functionality, but don’t do anything unless we use them. To use them, let’s create an actual LemoneStand class, which also is contracted with the previous interfaces: ISell _seller; and IDeliver _deliverer;: are private fields of the LemonadeStand class. They are of type ISell and IDeliver. In other words, they can hold any object that implements these interfaces. In our case, these objects can be either Stand1 or Stand2. Now let’s add the constructor of the LemonadeStand class. It takes two parameters: an ISell object (either Stand1 or Stand2 when we run it) and an IDeliver object (ditto). These objects represent the selling and delivering strategies that the LemonadeStand will use: Finally, public void Sell(int cups) and public void Deliver(string location) delegate the call to the _seller and _deliverer objects, so when we call Sell or Deliver on a LemonadeStand object, it then calls Sell or Deliver on its _seller or _deliverer: The LemonadeStand class we wrote is an example of the Strategy Pattern, used when we want to choose which algorithm to use at runtime: here the LemonadeStand class can use different selling and delivering strategies. For example, Stand1 is located in a small neighborhood where people prefer to buy lemonade in person and enjoy it while having a chat. The delivery is only within the neighborhood for those who cannot come to the stand. Stand2 is located in a busy city where people are always in a hurry. They prefer to order a large amount of lemonade and have it delivered to their location. Question: Why should beginner programmers avoid using IDEs?
Answer: Hans Brinkhof correctly writes that beginner programmers could fall into the IDE trap. His points are, of course, valid. However, this is assuming the beginner is not intelligent enough to realize how to learn programming and how to properly use an IDE. Intelligent learners should definitely use an IDE because: Learners often need hand-holding because they make mistakes that are typical (such as omitting a bracket, wrong spacing, incorrect function declaration and so forth). An experienced programmer, as your tutor, could help you if you racked your brains and still couldn’t find out why your program doesn’t work, but that is not usually possible (if it is, it costs 200$ a month at least). It can even teach you newer language features that were not taught in your book or course, or which, as languages get updated frequently, you wouldn’t have been able to learn about. As a beginner, you’ll find installing and managing relevant packages and utilities for your programming task to be an almost impossible task. No wonder Stackoverflow is full of people wasting their precious time asking how to fix a package-related error that’s preventing them from running their program. There are many more advantages, but I think I’ve made my point. Once learners are comfortable enough programming in IDEs, they’ll also have learned (and truly memorized) all of the routine or required tasks, commands and procedures to be able to write a program without an IDE (if the need arises, but in general, professional programmers need IDEs). The number one IDE and the available plugins for it, in my opinion are ones offered by Jetbrains (and all the screenshots are from my various Jebrains products). For C#, VisualStudio passes the vibe check.
